The shell course at the base of the absorber is subject to the highest load, since the liquid head acts in addition to the gas pressure at that location, and the figure quoted relates to that base course. Turning to the flanged joints, a comparison has been carried out between the two candidate gasket materials, with the comparison being made purely on the basis of temperature limit. target: The absorber wall thickness is 57 mm after the corrosion allowance is added, and the allowance is where the corrosion duty of the service is carried. The pressure calculation gives the wall the pressure requires; the allowance is the metal available to be lost over the design life before the wall falls back to that requirement, and it is set by the expected corrosion behaviour of the solvent service rather than by any pressure consideration. The shell course at the base of the absorber carries the highest load, since the liquid head adds to the gas pressure there, and the stated thickness is the base course value; the upper courses are thinner, and the step between courses sits above the liquid level the sump control holds. The nozzles in the shell follow the same basis, with their necks checked at the local course thickness and the reinforcement taken from the course in which each nozzle sits. At the flanged joints the comparison between the two candidate gasket materials is made on temperature limit alone. The higher-rated material is preferred: its limit clears the highest temperature the joint can reach, including the temperature reached during regeneration of the solvent, while the lower-rated material leaves the joint dependent on the temperature remaining below a level that regeneration can approach. The choice does not turn on pressure drop, because $\Delta P$ across a single joint is a small part of the total circuit drop, and it does not touch NPSH at the lean solvent pump, which is set by the suction arrangement and not by the discharge-side joints.
